h1: Columbus hops and the dank resin behind classic American IPAs
title: Columbus Hops and Dank Resin in IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: Columbus hops give dank resin, black pepper and citrus peel to classic American IPAs. Dosing, the CTZ name puzzle and how to avoid onion and hop creep.
teaser: Dank, resinous and peppery. Columbus is the hop behind a lot of classic American IPA.
standfirst: Columbus is a high alpha American hop sold under three names. It bitters hard and smells of resin, black pepper and citrus peel. This guide covers the dosing, the flavour and two faults to avoid.
sections:
Columbus is a high alpha American hop with alpha acids of roughly 14 to 18%. You will also see it sold as Tomahawk or Zeus. Brewers group the three as CTZ, because they behave as the same variety. The name on the bag often tells you more about the merchant than the hop, so judge each lot by its certificate of analysis.

It is a dual-purpose hop. At the start of the boil it gives clean, firm bitterness at a fair price per unit of alpha. In the whirlpool and the dry hop it gives the character that made it famous.
What dank means in the glass

Brewers use the word dank for a heavy, resinous, slightly earthy aroma. It comes from terpenes such as myrcene, humulene and caryophyllene. The same family of compounds gives cannabis its smell. Hops and cannabis are cousins in the plant family Cannabaceae.

Columbus adds black pepper, citrus peel and a deep pine note. It reads as old-school American IPA, the kind that came before the soft, juicy beers. If you want something fruitier, look at Strata, which pairs dank with passion fruit, or Rakau, which gives apricot over resin.

Bitterness first. For 1,000 L at 60 IBU, 1.6 kg of Columbus at 15% alpha and 25% utilisation gives about 60 IBU at 60 minutes (1,600 g x 0.15 x 0.25 x 1,000 / 1,000 L). That is a hard bitterness, so many brewers split it: 1 kg at the start for roughly 37 IBU, then the rest at 15 minutes and in the whirlpool for flavour.

Whirlpool at 80 °C for 20 minutes with 1 to 2 g per litre. Dry hop at 3 to 5 g per litre in total, at 18 to 20 °C. Columbus is strong. The dry hop is where its heaviness shows. Run a 20 L trial before you commit a full brew. Balance the resin with a citrus or tropical hop, so that the beer has a bright top note over the deep base.

The floor detail that matters most is whirlpool temperature. Above about 85 °C you drive off the lighter oils and extract a coarse bitterness. Let the wort settle to 80 °C, add the hops and stir gently for the first minutes so the pellets disperse instead of clumping.

At heavy rates, Columbus and related hops can give an onion or garlic note. Sulphur-containing compounds in the hop and their reactions in the beer are the cause. The risk grows with dry hop rate, contact time and old hop stock.

If you taste it, cut the dry hop rate, shorten contact to three days and check the age of the pellets. Blending with a fruity hop usually masks a mild case. A strong case means the beer is not saleable.

Hops carry enzymes that break down starch and dextrins into fermentable sugars. Added to a finished beer, they can restart fermentation. Brewers call it hop creep. It pushes gravity down, makes the beer stronger and raises carbonation in the package.

In a warm distribution chain the risk is real. Over-carbonated cans bulge and gush. Some burst. Confirm that fermentation has finished and that gravity is stable for two days before you package a dry hopped beer. Keep cans and kegs cold. Check for diacetyl as well, because refermentation can bring it back.

High alpha hops store better than aroma hops, but they still lose alpha in warmth. Keep pellets sealed in a cold room or freezer. Buy by the crop year. Ask your supplier for lab alpha, oil content and hop storage index, which measures ageing. A pack that has crossed an Indian summer in a van will not match the label.

If you are comparing a new batch with an older one, brew a split trial and taste both at the same temperature. Our Northern Brewer guide shows how a different kind of resin plays in a steam beer, which makes a useful contrast.
faqs: Are Columbus, Tomahawk and Zeus the same hop?
Brewers treat them as the same variety, grouped as CTZ. Sold under different names, they can differ slightly by farm and crop, so check the analysis.
What does dank mean in beer?
A heavy, resinous, earthy hop aroma caused by terpenes such as myrcene and humulene.
Can Columbus be used for bittering only?
Yes. Its high alpha acids make it a cost-effective bittering hop. Many brewers use it for that and nothing else.
